RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Jake is a 22-year-old CNA in a memory care unit. He is experienced with residents and music: during afternoon activities he plays only the first three tracks of Born in the U.S.A., then switches to quieter music because he has learned that too much stimulation can tip residents into agitation; he knows which residents hum, tap, or stare. He carries restless energy and has applied to travel nursing contracts in Anchorage, Fairbanks, and Nome; the brochures are in his locker. He tells himself Alaska is about wilderness and a real challenge, but he also knows it is about distance from the memory care unit, his parents' disappointment, and the business school he left after one semester. His father, a mechanical engineer, still says "when you go back for your degree"; his mother, a nurse practitioner, suggested CNA training and quietly hopes he will settle into something stable. He grew up in a middle-class Indianapolis suburb with a family culture of practical achievement: get the degree, get the job, get the house. His values are a tangle of that pragmatism and a newer, half-formed belief that meaning comes from showing up for people who are falling apart. He hates feeling hollow and useless after leaving a resident's room following a death, but he also hates the idea of doing anything else; the tension between wanting to stay and wanting to run keeps him moving and applying to remote jobs. A defining personal history remains: during his sophomore year of college, while staring at a marketing project spreadsheet, he felt physical revulsion so strong he closed the laptop and did not open it again; he called his mother at 2 a.m. crying, and she drove three hours to pick him up. The shame of needing rescue and the relief of being taken away still shape his decision-making: he does not want to need rescue again and wants to be the one who rescues, no matter how far he has to go.

He knows the night shift CNA as someone who always says thank you and once brought him a bagel after he covered for her. She has a young daughter and often needs last-minute coverage; he has provided it twice before. He feels a mild, unspoken obligation because she saved him from a difficult situation once when he forgot his badge.

His established tendencies around coverage requests are relevant: when he sees a note asking for coverage, he usually writes his name on it before finishing his coffee, even if tired. In the past three months, he has said yes to every shift trade requested unless he had a prior commitment. He often tells himself he will say no next time, but when the moment comes, he imagines the other person's relief and agrees.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

Jake arrives at the memory care unit fifteen minutes before his shift starts, as usual. The break room is empty except for a half-full pot of coffee and a note from the night shift CNA asking if anyone can cover the last hour of her shift tomorrow. Jake has already worked five doubles this month. The note and the coffee are before him; he can sit down with his coffee or respond to the note. He has not yet acted on either option.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

His body aches from the five doubles, especially his lower back and the balls of his feet. He is emotionally flat—not dreading the day but not energized by it. He has a small, constant headache from poor sleep and too much caffeine. Seeing the note, its handwriting reminds him of a similar request two weeks ago that led to an exhausting thirteen-hour day. Seeing the half-empty coffee pot cues a memory of the night he called his mother at 2 a.m., her voice steady as she said she would be there soon.
